::: {.lead}
A space station fires a mining beam at asteroids. The beam goes in one
direction. Which asteroid does it hit? Is an asteroid too far to the side?
Is it behind the station? In Lecture 2 you found the length of a vector, and
in Lecture 3 the dot product. In this lesson you put the two together to
answer the questions that games ask all the time: *which target is
nearest*, *how far along a road* or a beam is an object, *how much of a
movement goes into a wall*, and *does a shot hit*. The main new idea is the
**projection**: the part of a vector that goes along one direction. Every
section ends with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary distance projection perpendicular-part ray dot-product unit-vector magnitude surface-normal cross-product >}}

## 5.1 Which target is nearest?

A tower with auto-aim stands at $T = (2, 2)$. Three enemies come near:
E1 at $(5, 6)$, E2 at $(6, 2)$ and E3 at $(-1, -2)$. The tower shoots at the
nearest one. The game must find the **distance** to each enemy and compare.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.1 — Distance"}
The **distance** between two points $A$ and $B$ is the magnitude of the
vector from one to the other:
$$\text{distance}(A, B) = |B - A|.$$
In 2D: $\sqrt{(B_x - A_x)^2 + (B_y - A_y)^2}$. In 3D, add the $z$-part.
:::

![The distances from the tower to three enemies. The squares are enough to compare.](images/nearest.png){#fig-nearest width=94%}

The game does not need the exact distances to find the nearest enemy. A
bigger distance always has a bigger square. So the game compares
$x^2 + y^2$ and skips the square roots.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.1 — The nearest enemy"}
The tower is at $T = (2, 2)$ (@fig-nearest).

1. E1: $\mathbf{d} = (3, 4)$, $3^2 + 4^2 = 25$, distance 5.
2. E2: $\mathbf{d} = (4, 0)$, $4^2 + 0^2 = 16$, distance 4.
3. E3: $\mathbf{d} = (-3, -4)$, $9 + 16 = 25$, distance 5.
4. The smallest square is 16: the tower aims at **E2**. E1 and E3 are
   equally far, in opposite directions.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Comparing only one coordinate. E2 at $(6, 2)$ has a bigger $x$ than E1 at
$(5, 6)$, but it is nearer to the tower. Distance uses *all* the parts of the
vector, and it starts at the tower, not at the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Distances in GeoGebra"}
Open geogebra.org/calculator.

1. Type `T = (2, 2)`, `E1 = (5, 6)`, `E2 = (6, 2)` and `E3 = (-1, -2)`.
2. Type `Distance(T, E1)`, and the same for E2 and E3.
3. Which enemy is nearest? Check one distance by hand.

*Your result:* three distances, the nearest enemy, and your check.

::: {.check}
Distances 5, 4 and 5: E2 is nearest. Check E2 by hand: $(6, 2) - (2, 2) =
(4, 0)$, length $\sqrt{16} = 4$.
:::
:::

## 5.2 How far along the road?

A racing game shows the progress of each car: "7 m along the road". The road
starts at $S$ and goes straight in the direction of the unit vector
$\hat{\mathbf{u}}$. A car is never exactly on the centre line. So the game
asks: how far *along the road* is the car? The answer is the length of the
car's "shadow" on the road (@fig-proj).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.2 — Projection on a direction"}
The **projection** of a vector $\mathbf{v}$ on a direction $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$
(a unit vector) is the part of $\mathbf{v}$ that goes along
$\hat{\mathbf{u}}$. Its length with a sign is
$$\text{along} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}.$$
It is negative when $\mathbf{v}$ points backwards.
:::

![The car at (5, 5) and its shadow on a road in the direction (0.6, 0.8): 7 units along.](images/projection.png){#fig-proj width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.2 — Progress on a straight road"}
The road starts at $S = (0, 0)$ and goes along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (1, 0)$.

1. A car at $(7, 2)$: $\mathbf{v} = (7, 2)$, and
   $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = 7$. It is 7 units along the road.
   The 2 units to the side do not count.
2. A car at $(-3, 1)$: $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = -3$. It is 3
   units *behind* the start.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.3 — A diagonal road"}
The road starts at $S = (0, 0)$ and goes along
$\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0.6, 0.8)$. A car is at $P = (5, 5)$.

1. $\mathbf{v} = P - S = (5, 5)$.
2. $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = 5 \times 0.6 + 5 \times 0.8 = 3 + 4 = 7$.
3. The car is 7 units along the road. It is also a little to the side,
   but that part does not count as progress.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using a direction that is not a unit vector. With $(3, 4)$ instead of
$(0.6, 0.8)$, the car at $(5, 5)$ gives $15 + 20 = 35$: five times too much.
Normalize the direction first.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
Vector2 toCar = car - roadStart;
float along = Vector2.Dot(toCar, roadDir.normalized);   // 7
```
:::

{{< sim file="sims/projection-lab.html" poster="sims/projection-lab.png" title="Projection Lab: along, across and slide" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Along the road in Projection Lab"}
Open the **Projection Lab** simulator above (or scan its QR code).

1. Choose $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0.6, 0.8)$. Drag the tip of $\mathbf{v}$ to
   $(5, 5)$, $(3, 4)$ and $(-3, -4)$.
2. Each time, write the value "along".

*Your result:* three rows, and one sentence: when is "along" negative?

::: {.check}
$(5, 5)$: 7. $(3, 4)$: $1.8 + 3.2 = 5$. $(-3, -4)$: $-5$. "Along" is negative
when $\mathbf{v}$ points backwards, behind the start of the road.
:::
:::

## 5.3 Along and across: splitting a vector

A plane in a flight game flies along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (1, 0)$. The wind
blows with $\mathbf{w} = (3, 4)$. Part of the wind pushes the plane forward;
the other part pushes it off its course. The game splits the wind into two
parts at a right angle to each other (@fig-split).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.3 — The parts along and across"}
For a vector $\mathbf{v}$ and a unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$:
$$\mathbf{v}_{\text{along}} = (\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}})\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_{\text{across}} = \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{along}}.$$
The part across is the **perpendicular part**. The two parts add up to
$\mathbf{v}$.
:::

![v = (5, 0) split along û = (0.6, 0.8) and across it.](images/along-across.png){#fig-split width=92%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.4 — Wind on a plane"}
The plane flies along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (1, 0)$. The wind is
$\mathbf{w} = (3, 4)$.

1. $\mathbf{w} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = 3$, so the part along is
   $3 \times (1, 0) = (3, 0)$: it speeds the plane up.
2. The part across is $(3, 4) - (3, 0) = (0, 4)$: it pushes the plane off
   its course.
3. To stay on course, the pilot must steer against $(0, 4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing the part along as a number. $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = 3$ is
its *length*. The part along is a vector: $3 \times \hat{\mathbf{u}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Split a vector"}
In **Projection Lab**, choose $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0.8, 0.6)$ and drag
$\mathbf{v}$ to $(5, 0)$.

1. Write the part along and the part across from the cards.
2. Add the two parts on paper. Do you get $(5, 0)$?

*Your result:* the two parts and your sum.

::: {.check}
$\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = 4$; along $4 \times (0.8, 0.6) = (3.2, 2.4)$;
across $(5, 0) - (3.2, 2.4) = (1.8, -2.4)$. The sum is $(5, 0)$.
:::
:::

### Sliding along a wall

The same split solves a common problem. A player runs diagonally into the floor of a level with the velocity
$\mathbf{v} = (3, -4)$. If the game stops the player completely, the
movement feels sticky. If it does nothing, the player sinks into the floor.
Most games do a third thing: they remove only the part of the movement that
goes *into* the floor, and the player slides along it (@fig-slide).

The floor has the unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ (Lecture 4). The part of
$\mathbf{v}$ along the normal is $(\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}})\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.
When $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} < 0$, the player moves into the
floor, and the game takes this part away:
$$\mathbf{v}_{\text{slide}} = \mathbf{v} - (\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}})\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}.$$
This is the perpendicular part, with the normal as the direction.

![The player moves into the floor. The game removes the part along the normal, and the player slides.](images/wall-slide.png){#fig-slide width=92%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.5 — Landing on the floor"}
The floor has $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (0, 1)$. The player moves with
$\mathbf{v} = (3, -4)$.

1. $\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 3 \times 0 + (-4) \times 1 = -4$.
   Negative: into the floor.
2. $\mathbf{v}_{\text{slide}} = (3, -4) - (-4) \times (0, 1) = (3, -4) + (0, 4) = (3, 0)$.
3. The player keeps moving right at 3 units per frame, on the floor.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A sign error: $(3, -4) + (-4) \times (0, 1) = (3, -8)$. This pushes the player
*deeper* into the floor. The formula *subtracts*
$(\mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}})\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, and minus a negative
number adds.
:::

## 5.4 Will the shot hit?

A turret fires a laser along a straight line. Games call such a line a
**ray**. An enemy has a round body with the radius 1. Does the ray hit it?
The game checks three things for the vector $\mathbf{d}$ from the turret to
the enemy (@fig-ray):

1. **in front:** along $= \mathbf{d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} > 0$;
2. **in range:** along $\le$ the range of the laser;
3. **close to the line:** the length of the part across is at most the
   radius.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 5.4 — Ray"}
A **ray** starts at a point and goes on in one direction $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$.
Games use rays to test what a shot, a beam or a line of sight hits.
:::

In 2D there is a short way to find the length of the part across. It is the
2D cross product of Lecture 4, without its sign:
$$\text{across} = |\hat{u}_x d_y - \hat{u}_y d_x|.$$

![A ray from the turret along (1, 0). E1 is hit, E2 is too far to the side, and E3 is behind.](images/ray-hit.png){#fig-ray width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.6 — Three enemies"}
The turret is at $(0, 0)$ and fires along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (1, 0)$. The
range is 10 and the radius is 1.

1. E1 at $(6, 1)$: along 6, across 1. $0 < 6 \le 10$ and $1 \le 1$: **hit**.
2. E2 at $(4, 3)$: along 4, across 3. $3 > 1$: **miss**, too far to the side.
3. E3 at $(-5, 0)$: along $-5$: **miss**, it is behind.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the distance to the enemy. E2 in Example 5.6 is 5 units from
the turret, closer than E1 (about 6). But the ray misses E2, because it is 3
units to the side.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Hit or miss on paper"}
A turret at $(0, 0)$ fires along $(1, 0)$ with the range 8. Each enemy has the
radius 1. The enemies are at $(5, 0)$, $(3, 2)$, $(9, 0)$ and $(-2, 1)$.

1. For each enemy, find "along" and "across".
2. Mark each one "hit" or "miss", with the reason.

*Your result:* a table with four rows.

::: {.check}
$(5, 0)$: along 5, across 0: hit. $(3, 2)$: across 2 > 1: miss (to the
side). $(9, 0)$: along 9 > 8: miss (out of range). $(-2, 1)$: along −2: miss
(behind).
:::
:::

## Case study: Asteroid Beam

*Asteroid Beam* is a made-up mining game. A station at $S = (1, 1)$ fires a
beam along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0.6, 0.8)$. The beam is 10 units long, and
each asteroid has the radius 1. Three asteroids float near the beam:
A at $(4, 5)$, B at $(5, 4)$ and C at $(7, 9)$. The beam stops at the first
asteroid it hits. The player must say which one. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses these numbers. In the mini-game below you solve five
rounds with other stations and directions.

{{< sim file="sims/asteroid-beam.html" poster="sims/asteroid-beam.png" title="Asteroid Beam: which asteroid does the beam hit first?" kind="game" height="760" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*,
2nd ed., Chapter 2 ("Vectors"): the distance formula, and the projection of
one vector onto another with its perpendicular part.

## Exercises

1. Find the distance between $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$.
2. A tower at $(0, 0)$. Enemies at $(6, 8)$, $(-5, 5)$ and $(0, -9)$. Which one
   is nearest? Compare the squares.
3. Find the distance between $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(3, 4, 7)$.
4. A road starts at $(0, 0)$ and goes along $(0, 1)$. How far along the road is
   a car at $(2, 9)$? And a car at $(1, -4)$?
5. A road goes along $(0.8, 0.6)$ from $(0, 0)$. How far along is a car at
   $(5, 5)$?
6. Why must the direction be a unit vector in the projection?
7. Split $\mathbf{v} = (4, 6)$ along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0, 1)$.
8. Split $\mathbf{v} = (0, 5)$ along $\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (0.6, 0.8)$. Check
   that the part across is perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$.
9. A player moves with $(4, -2)$ onto a floor with $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (0, 1)$.
   Find the slide.
10. A wall on the left faces right: $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (1, 0)$. The player
    moves with $(-3, 2)$. Find the slide.
11. A player moves with $(2, 5)$ near a floor with $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (0, 1)$.
    Does the game change the movement? Why?
12. A turret at $(0, 0)$ fires along $(0, 1)$, range 10, radius 1. Is an enemy
    at $(1, 6)$ hit? An enemy at $(3, 4)$? An enemy at $(0, -4)$?
13. A beam from $(0, 0)$ along $(0.6, 0.8)$. An enemy at $(4, 3)$ has
    "along" 4.8. What is "across"? Is it hit (radius 1)?
14. *Asteroid Beam*: which asteroid does the beam hit first, and why does it
    not hit B?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. d = (3, 4); √(9 + 16) = 5.
2. Squares: 100, 50, 81. The smallest square is 50: (−5, 5) is nearest.
3. d = (2, 3, 6); √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7.
4. (2, 9): 9 units along. (1, −4): −4, so 4 units behind the start.
5. 5 × 0.8 + 5 × 0.6 = 4 + 3 = 7.
6. Otherwise the dot product is multiplied by the length of the direction, and the result is too big (or too small).
7. v · û = 6; along (0, 6); across (4, 0).
8. v · û = 4; along 4 × (0.6, 0.8) = (2.4, 3.2); across (0, 5) − (2.4, 3.2) = (−2.4, 1.8). Check: −2.4 × 0.6 + 1.8 × 0.8 = −1.44 + 1.44 = 0.
9. v · n̂ = −2; slide = (4, −2) − (−2)(0, 1) = (4, 0).
10. v · n̂ = −3; slide = (−3, 2) − (−3)(1, 0) = (0, 2): the player slides up.
11. No. v · n̂ = 5 > 0: the player moves away from the floor.
12. (1, 6): along 6, across 1: hit. (3, 4): along 4, across 3: miss. (0, −4): along −4: behind, miss.
13. across = |0.6 × 3 − 0.8 × 4| = |1.8 − 3.2| = 1.4 > 1: miss.
14. A (along 5, across 0). B is 1.4 units across, more than the radius 1. C is on the line too, but farther (along 10), so the beam stops at A.
:::
